title: ICT Skills and Working in Linux

sections.title: Mission · Everyday Linux and ICT Skills
paragraphs: This objective connects basic computer skills with everyday Linux usage.
bullets: Industry uses of Linux, cloud computing, and virtualization
Browser usage, configuration, searching, saving content, and privacy
Open-source applications in presentations and projects
sections.callout: USE LINUX THROUGH THE DESKTOP, COMMAND LINE, CLOUD, AND VIRTUAL SYSTEMS

sections.title: Desktop Skills
paragraphs: Linux can provide graphical desktop environments where users interact with windows, menus, icons, files, applications, settings, and web browsers. Using Linux does not mean everything must happen in a terminal. A Linux user may work through both a GUI and the command line.
sections.callout: LINUX CAN USE GUI + COMMAND LINE

sections.title: Using a Browser
paragraphs: Basic ICT skills include navigating websites, searching the web, saving content, downloading files, configuring browser options, and understanding privacy implications. Firefox is one open-source browser from Objective 1.2.
sections.callout: A browser is both a productivity tool and a privacy boundary.

sections.title: Searching the Web
paragraphs: Administrators frequently search for documentation, error messages, configuration instructions, software information, and troubleshooting information. Search results must be evaluated carefully because not every result is accurate or trustworthy.
sections.callout: SEARCH, THEN EVALUATE THE SOURCE

sections.title: Saving Content
paragraphs: Browsers can save or download content from the web. Before downloading or executing content, consider the source, trustworthiness, file type, security, and privacy. Downloading something is not the same as knowing it is safe.
sections.callout: DOWNLOAD DOES NOT MEAN TRUSTED

sections.title: Privacy Concerns
paragraphs: Internet services can expose browsing activity, accounts, location, preferences, devices, and personal data. Convenience and privacy can involve tradeoffs.
sections.callout: THINK ABOUT WHAT DATA A SERVICE COLLECTS OR STORES

sections.title: Browser Configuration Options
paragraphs: Browser settings can affect privacy, cookies, history, saved passwords, downloads, search providers, extensions, and security behavior. The exam expects general awareness rather than mastery of one browser's menu structure.
sections.callout: Configuration choices affect convenience, security, and privacy.

sections.title: Getting to the Command Line
paragraphs: A major Linux skill is knowing how to access a command-line environment. You may encounter the terms terminal and console.
sections.callout: COMMAND-LINE ACCESS MAY COME THROUGH A TERMINAL OR CONSOLE

sections.title: Terminal
paragraphs: A terminal provides an interface through which a user can interact with a shell and enter commands. On a graphical Linux desktop, a terminal emulator can open in a window.
sections.callout: TERMINAL = PLACE TO TYPE COMMANDS

sections.title: Console
paragraphs: A console generally refers to direct system interaction through a text-oriented interface or session. At Linux Essentials level, recognize that terminals and consoles can both provide command-line access.
sections.callout: CONSOLE = DIRECT OR TEXT-ORIENTED SYSTEM INTERACTION

sections.title: Why the Command Line Matters
paragraphs: The Linux command line enables remote administration, automation, precise control, fast system management, and access on systems without graphical desktops. Many Linux servers operate without a traditional desktop interface.
sections.callout: COMMAND-LINE SKILLS ARE CORE LINUX SKILLS

sections.title: Password Issues
paragraphs: Passwords protect user accounts and resources. Common concerns include weak passwords, reused passwords, shared passwords, exposed passwords, and poor storage practices. A password should not be treated casually just because the machine is personal.
sections.callout: STRONG, UNIQUE, PRIVATE PASSWORDS PROTECT ACCOUNTS

sections.title: Privacy Issues and Tools
paragraphs: Privacy applies to local files, accounts, web browsing, communications, cloud services, and shared systems. Privacy tools and configuration options can reduce unnecessary exposure, but users still need good judgment.
sections.callout: TOOLS HELP; JUDGMENT STILL MATTERS

sections.title: Linux in Industry
paragraphs: Linux is used in servers, web hosting, networking, cloud computing, software development, embedded systems, supercomputing, and automation. Linux skills remain useful even when someone's everyday desktop runs another operating system.
sections.callout: LINUX POWERS MANY PROFESSIONAL TECHNOLOGY ENVIRONMENTS

sections.title: Cloud Computing
paragraphs: Cloud computing provides computing resources through remotely hosted infrastructure and services. Linux is widely used for cloud workloads. A Linux cloud server may be created remotely, managed over a network, used without a physical monitor, and administered primarily through a command line.
sections.callout: CLOUD + LINUX = COMMON INDUSTRY COMBINATION

sections.title: Virtualization
paragraphs: Virtualization allows multiple virtual systems to run using physical computing resources. A virtual machine can run Linux even when the underlying physical computer uses another operating system. Virtualization is important for testing, labs, development, servers, and cloud infrastructure.

entries.title: Scenario
paragraphs: A Windows computer runs an Ubuntu virtual machine. Ubuntu is still a complete Linux operating environment even though the hardware is virtualized.
entries.recognitionCue: Linux guest running as a virtual computer → Virtualization

sections.title: Exam Trap — Cloud vs. Virtualization
paragraphs: Cloud platforms commonly use virtualization underneath, but the terms are not interchangeable.

table.caption: Separate the delivery model from the enabling technology
rows: Deliver computing resources and services remotely

sections.title: Open-Source Applications in Projects
paragraphs: Open-source applications support professional and educational work: LibreOffice for documents and presentations, Firefox for research, GIMP for graphics, and Thunderbird for email. Linux knowledge includes both command-line administration and ordinary productivity skills.
sections.callout: OPEN-SOURCE TOOLS SUPPORT EVERYDAY PROJECT WORK

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Graphical access to applications and files → Desktop or GUI
Type Linux commands → Terminal or console
Manage a server without a graphical desktop → Command line
Change browser cookie, history, or privacy behavior → Browser configuration and privacy
Linux server on remotely hosted infrastructure → Cloud computing
Ubuntu runs as a VM on another operating system → Virtualization
sections.callout: Recognize the interface, environment, and user need.

sections.title: GSA Exam Traps

entries.title: GUI vs. CLI
paragraphs: GUI means graphical interaction. CLI means text commands. Both can exist on the same Linux machine.

entries.title: Terminal vs. Shell
paragraphs: A terminal is the interface or environment used to enter commands. A shell is the command interpreter that processes them.

entries.title: Cloud vs. Virtualization
paragraphs: Cloud means remotely delivered computing resources or services. Virtualization means virtualized computers or resources.

entries.title: Convenience vs. Privacy
paragraphs: A browser feature can be convenient while also storing or sharing information. Treat privacy as a separate consideration.

sections.callout: INTERFACE · INTERPRETER · DELIVERY · VIRTUALIZATION · PRIVACY

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Direct or text system interaction → Console
Documents and presentations → Open-source productivity applications
sections.callout: CLICK = GUI · TYPE = TERMINAL · INTERPRET = SHELL · PROTECT = PASSWORD · REMOTE = CLOUD · VIRTUAL COMPUTER = VM

bullets: Enterprise Linux → Red Hat or SUSE
Web servers → Apache HTTPD or NGINX
Red Hat packages → rpm or yum
